Rhombic Skaapsteker neonates emerge from parchment-shelled eggs with a relatively modest size. Upon hatching, these hatchlings typically measure approximately 19 centimeters [Lb = approximately 19 centimeters] in total length, a dimension that reflects the constraints of the cleidoic egg environment. The eggs themselves, which are leathery-shelled, exhibit an initial egg weight of 2.94 grams [Ww0 = 2.94 grams], a value derived from the typical dimensions of the oviposited clutch. This modest mass at oviposition supports the yolk-dependent embryo through its developmental period until eclosion. The incubation duration, when maintained at a constant temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C], spans approximately 42 days [ab = approximately 42 days] before the shell pipping event occurs. This period of embryonic development is comparable to that observed in other psammophiine snakes, where thermal conditions strongly influence the rate of yolk absorption and subsequent emergence of the hatchling.

As the juvenile snake grows and transitions toward exogenous feeding, it embarks on a period of rapid somatic expansion. The maximum total length recorded for this species approaches 140 centimeters [Li = 140 centimeters], a size that places the rhombic skaapsteker among the larger members of its genus. In terms of mass, the ultimate weight recorded in adults reaches approximately 1.9 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 1.9 kilograms], though most individuals in the field fall somewhat below this asymptotic value. This substantial body mass, calculated from comparative data on Psammophis sibilans, represents the upper limit of adult size and likely reflects the species' capacity to exploit abundant prey resources in its grassland and fynbos habitats. Comparable data from congeneric species suggest that this maximum weight is attained only after several years of sustained feeding, with males typically remaining smaller than females throughout their lives.

The transition from juvenile to reproductive adult is marked by the attainment of a specific body length. Field surveys indicate that the total length at puberty for Psammophylax rhombeatus is approximately 70 centimeters [Lp = approximately 70 centimeters], although individual variation is considerable, with some populations documenting onset of gonadal activation at lengths ranging between 45 and 85 centimeters. This length threshold corresponds to the point at which gametogenesis onset occurs and individuals become capable of their first copulation. The age at which this length is reached depends strongly on local prey availability and thermal conditions, but most sub-adult individuals in optimal habitats achieve this size within their second or third year after emergence from the egg. Reaching this developmental milestone is a prerequisite for participating in the breeding population and for producing the first egg clutch.

Reproductive output in this oviparous species, when measured at the thermal conditions typical of its active season (30 °C [T = 30 °C]), is characterized by a moderate clutch size and relatively infrequent breeding events. During the active season, females produce approximately 30 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 30 eggs per clutch], a substantial fecundity that reflects the species' ability to allocate significant resources toward offspring production. These clutches are deposited in shallow nests within sandy soil or under rock cover. Under these same thermal conditions, females typically produce two clutches per year [F_R_i = two clutches per year], yielding a maximum reproductive output that supports population persistence in variable environments. The combination of these two parameters, a large clutch size and a biannual laying frequency, gives the species a relatively high annual reproductive potential compared to other African colubrids of similar body size.

Longevity data for the rhombic skaapsteker, derived primarily from captive individuals and extrapolations from the congener Psammophis subtaeniatus, indicate a maximum life span of approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] when maintained at a constant temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C]. In the wild, this figure is likely lower due to predation pressure from avian raptors and mammalian carnivores, as well as the energetic costs of reproduction and seasonal resource limitation. The species demonstrates a gradual senescence pattern, with older individuals showing reduced feeding rates and slower locomotor performance. This maximum longevity, equivalent to roughly 2190 days, represents the upper bound of physiological lifespan for this snake under captive conditions and provides a useful benchmark for comparative life-history studies among African psammophiine snakes.
